x-ray with evidence of pneumonia.

HOSPITAL COURSE BY ISSUE/SYSTEM:  The patient was admitted to

treatment.

intravenous fluids and levofloxacin for her pneumonia.  In

left-sided effusion under ultrasound guidance, but this only

chest x-ray several days later revealed right-sided
infiltrates in the upper and medial lung zones and a small
right-sided effusion as well.

chest computerized axial tomography to further evaluate her
effusion and pneumonia.

trachea carina and proximal main stem bronchi which was

metastatic workup for an adenocystic carcinoma of the carina

Hematology/Oncology, and Thoracic Surgery teams who deemed
the patient should be followed as an outpatient for further

patient off of assist control and was successfully weaned
down a pressure support of 15 and 5.

for nearly three weeks from the time she initially presented
to an outside hospital, on hospital day 18, the patient had
tracheostomy placed after discussion with the family.  The
patient was maintained on pressure support after that, and on
the day of discharge was doing well on a pressure support of
13 and 10 with a plan to continue weaning her off the
ventilator slowly and decreasing the pressure support and the
elevation of the positive end-expiratory pressure.  The
patient's compliance remained in the high teens which she was
on assist control of unclear etiology; likely due to chest
wall decreased motion.

bilateral pleural effusions (medium on the right to small on

loculated with several pockets of air but minimal enhancement

collapse of the right lower lobe with patchy opacities in the
bilateral upper lobes and right middle lobe slightly
improved.  The patient was followed on plain films with a
slight improvement of the bilateral pleural effusions.  No
further taps were done at this time given all previous
cultures had remained negative, and the patient was
maintaining a low-grade fever.  The plan was if the patient
continued to spike fevers that these effusions would be
tapped and new cultures would be obtained.

bronchoscopy was performed to evaluate the left lower lobe
and showed thick mucous in the endotracheal tube, but no
mucous plugging or purulence in the left lower lobe.

pneumococcal pneumonia and continued to spike despite being
on clindamycin and ceftriaxone.  On hospital day 12, the
patient spiked fevers again to 101 with a question of a
ventilator-associated pneumonia, and ceftriaxone was
discontinued in favor of starting Zosyn for
ventilator-associated pneumonia.  Cultures were obtained
again, and at the time of discharge were still pending;
including fungal cultures.

catheter tip was sent for culture with no further growth.

clindamycin (on the day of discharge was on day 17) and Zosyn
for 10 days (on the day of discharge was on day four) for
continued pneumococcal ventilator-associated pneumonia.  If
the patient continues to spike, the patient should be further
evaluated for aspiration and have cultures followed up.

despite Zosyn and clindamycin during her hospitalization.

time of discharge.  The plan was that if the patient
continued to spike fevers again to consider an Infectious
Disease consultation and to re-tap the bilateral pleural
effusions.

pending at this time.  Other sources of fever should also be
considered if the patient re-spikes.

patient's hematocrit continued to drop.  On hospital day 14,
her hematocrit was 21.  Iron studies were sent which showed a
decreased total iron-binding capacity, and elevated ferritin,

anemia of chronic disease compounded by anemia of iron
deficiency.  The patient was started on epoetin alfa and iron

two units of packed red blood cells with a stable hematocrit

with intravenous fluids while the patient was nothing by

nutritional status was monitored, and the patient (as
dictated in fluids/electrolytes/nutrition below) was
maintained on total parenteral nutrition and tube feeds.

hospitalization while her tube feeds were slowly being
advanced.  Two days prior to discharge, her tube feeds were
at goal, and total parenteral nutrition was discontinued.

recommended that total parenteral nutrition was not indicated
at this time while the patient was at goal tube feeds.  On
the day prior to discharge, the patient had a percutaneous
endoscopic gastrostomy tube placed and was to be started on
the day of discharge with her goal tube feeds.  The patient's
electrolytes were repleted aggressively during this
hospitalization.

were all discontinued on the day prior to discharge.  The
patient had a peripherally inserted central catheter line
placed on [**9-18**] on the right side with two lumens.

tube placed on the day prior to discharge which was to be
started on the day of discharge.

subcutaneous heparin for deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis.
Famotidine was placed in her total parenteral nutrition for
gastrointestinal prophylaxis.  When total parenteral
nutrition was discontinued, the patient was begun on by mouth
famotidine.

10.  COMMUNICATION ISSUES:  Communication was with her mother
who was her health care proxy.  [**Name (NI) **] mother was updated on
daily events including the tracheostomy placement,
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube placement, and human
immunodeficiency virus antibody test.

11.  CODE STATUS:  The patient was maintained on full code
during this hospitalization.

12.  PSYCHIATRIC ISSUES:  The patient with a history of
substance abuse, and narcotic abuse, and anorexia, and
question depression.  The patient did not have a psychiatric
evaluation given the fact that she was intubated and unable
to talk.

On the day prior to discharge, we consulted Psychiatry for
management of her depression and her anorexia.  Psychiatry
had not been by to drop a note, and suggestions were still
pending.

The patient was maintained on Zyprexa (oral disintegrating
tablets) for agitation at night.  The patient was initially
sedated with an Ativan drip which was then changed to Ativan
around the clock with improvement of her anxiety throughout
her hospital stay.  The patient was maintained on a Fentanyl
patch for a history of polysubstance and narcotic abuse.

today to a rehabilitation facility pending location to be

1.  Known three-vessel coronary artery disease.  Last cardiac

descending stenosis, 90% RLA stenosis, 50% proximal stenosis
of the left circumflex and tight stenosis in D1 and D2.  The
patient also had a positive stress test.
2.  Hypertension.

1.  Insulin 70/30, 40 units twice a day.

bilaterally.  Heart examination is regular rate and rhythm

Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended with bowel sounds
present, no masses.  Extremities with no edema.  One plus
dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally.

count 5.3, platelets 268.  Sodium 139, BUN 10, creatinine
0.8, glucose 137.

Creatinine kinase 148, creatinine kinase MB fraction 2,
troponin less than 0.3.

EKG performed at the time of admission showed normal sinus
rhythm with flat T waves in leads II, III, AVF, V1, V3 and
V6.  No ST changes were seen.  No Q waves were seen.

the day of the patient's admission to Medicine.  She was seen
by Dr. [**First Name8 (NamePattern2) **] [**Last Name (NamePattern1) 1537**].  It was thought that the patient would
be a good surgical candidate for a coronary artery bypass
graft.  Her preoperative evaluation was performed including a
chest x-ray and additional laboratories.

bypass graft times four, left internal mammary artery to left
anterior descending, saphenous vein graft to patent ductus
arteriosus, saphenous vein graft to obtuse marginal,
saphenous vein graft to diagonal.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no
complications.  Please see the full Operative Note for
details.

stable condition.  Neurologically, the patient was responsive

sinus rhythm.

regular floor.  Her chest tube was removed.  Her diet was
advanced as tolerated.  She was vigorously diuresed with
Lasix.  On postoperative day two, the patient continued to do
well.  She was doing well on room air without any
supplemental oxygen.  Her pacing wires were removed on
postoperative day two.  Her urine catheter was removed on
postoperative day two as well.

elevated fingersticks.  Her insulin regimen was consequently
adjusted.  The patient was also placed on Plavix.  Physical
Therapy was consulted, who followed the patient throughout
her hospitalization.  The patient was cleared by Physical
Therapy to go home.  The patient was maintained on Lopressor
which was gradually increased to control her heart rate.

The patient was discharged to home on [**2196-11-4**].  Prior to
discharge the patient was noted to have a small amount of
serous drainage out of her chest wound.  At the time, it was
thought that there was no need for further intervention, but
close monitoring of the incision site was warranted.  The
patient was consequently discharged to home on an oral
antibiotic.

CONDITION ON DISCHARGE:   Good.

DISCHARGE DISPOSITION:   Home with services.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  Coronary artery disease status post coronary artery
bypass graft times four.
2.  Hypertension.
3.  Diabetes mellitus type 1.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
1.  Aspirin 325 mg p.o. q. day.

3.  Colace 100 mg p.o. twice a day.
4.  Keflex 500 mg p.o. q. six hours times 14 days.

8.  Percocet one to two tablets p.o. q. four to six hours

2.  The patient is to follow-up with her primary care
physician in approximately one to two weeks.
3.  The patient is to be referred to a Cardiologist by her
primary care physician as instructed and to be seen within
the next three to four weeks.
4.  The patient is to follow-up with her diabetes specialist.
5.  The patient is to be visited by Visiting Nurses

disease, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus.  He presented

occlusion of his proximal left anterior descending artery, a
90% occlusion of his distal left anterior descending artery,
a 90% occlusion of his left circumflex, a 100% occlusion of

20% to 25%.  He was also noted to have a left ventricular
aneurysm.

The patient was subsequently transferred to the [**Hospital1 346**] for management of his severe
coronary artery disease.

1.  He had an inferior myocardial infarction in [**2142**] that was
treated with thrombolysis.
2.  He had an anterior wall myocardial infarction in [**2143**] and
was treated with a percutaneous transluminal coronary
angioplasty of his left anterior descending artery.
3.  He has peripheral vascular disease, status post right
femoral stent in [**2153**].
4.  Hypercholesterolemia.
5.  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

accident.

revealed the patient was alert and oriented.  He was
neurologically intact.  He had a regular rate and rhythm.
His lungs were clear.  His abdomen was soft, nontender, and
nondistended.  His extremities were warm and well perfused.
His lower extremity veins appeared within normal limits
without varicosity or venous stasis changes.

HOSPITAL COURSE:   The patient was admitted to the
Cardiothoracic Service on [**2153-8-28**].  Adequate
resuscitation of his hemodynamic condition was carried out
overnight.

On hospital day two, the patient underwent and uncomplicated
repair of his left ventricular aneurysm as well as a coronary
artery bypass graft consisting of the left internal mammary
artery to the first obtuse marginal branch, and the saphenous
vein graft to the second obtuse marginal branch.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well and was taken to the
Cardiothoracic Intensive Care Unit intubated and in stable
condition.

Postoperatively, the patient was noted to have two runs of
ventricular tachycardia.  His magnesium and potassium levels
were repleted, and he was bolused with lidocaine and was
started on a lidocaine drip at 2 mg per minute.  He was
weaned from the ventilator and extubated without incident.
He was loaded with amiodarone overnight while remaining
atrial paced with an underlying sinus rhythm at a rate in
the 70s.

On the morning of postoperative day one, the patient went
into ventricular tachycardia at a rate in the 170s with a
systolic blood pressure drop to the 50s.  Lidocaine was
given, and the patient was cardioverted at 200 with immediate
conversion to sinus rhythm.  The patient continued to require
supplemental oxygen with a face mask at 60% in order to
maintain his oxygen saturations.  He was making good urine.

On postoperative day two, the patient had an episode of flash
pulmonary edema treated with 40 mg of intravenous Lasix.  He
remained on the nonrebreather with an oxygen saturation
of 93%.  The Electrophysiology Service had consulted on him
and recommended that the ventricular tachycardia could be
suppressed by atrially pacing him and continuing the
amiodarone.

On postoperative day three, the patient continued to require
supplemental oxygen.  He had an episode of slow ventricular
tachycardia at a rate of 150 that was treated with lidocaine
and Versed, and the rhythm was subsequently successfully
treated with rapid atrial pacing at 200.  A chest x-ray at
that time was notable for severe pulmonary edema, and his
face mask was changed to a 100% nonrebreather with oxygen
saturations still only in the 80% to 90% range.  He was begun
on an aggressive Lasix diuresis with good affect.

On postoperative day four, the patient was noted to be having
a continued oxygen requirement on 100% nonrebreather with
marginal arterial blood gases.  He had persistent increase in
work of breathing, and the decision was made to be
reintubated.  The patient underwent a transesophageal
echocardiogram which demonstrated no VEA while being both on
and off atrial pacing.

The patient continued to be plagued by brief episodes of
ventricular tachycardia responsive to rapid atrial pacing.
On postoperative day seven, the patient underwent placement
of a intra-aortic balloon pump.  At that time, a plan was
initiated to hold lidocaine while monitoring for ventricular
tachycardia with 12 lead pads in place for the purpose of
obtaining a 12-lead electrocardiogram which may allow for
identifying a focus for future ablation.  The patient
remained intubated and ventilated with no remarkable changes
in respiratory status.

On postoperative day eight, the patient was initiated on
total parenteral nutrition.  On postoperative day nine, the
patient underwent cardiac mapping of his ventricular
arrhythmias in the Electrophysiology laboratory.  Based on
these results he underwent multiple ablations of what
appeared to be the fossae of his arrhythmias.  He tolerated
the procedure well and was subsequently transported back to
the Cardiothoracic Intensive Care Unit in stable condition
with all external pacing off and on a Pronestyl drip.

On postoperative day 10, the patient remained sedated and
intubated.  His intra-aortic balloon pump was discontinued,
and he was started on tube feeds.  The patient was noted to
have an increasing white blood cell count, and so his central
lines were replaced.  Throughout the day he was successfully
weaned to CPAP with 5 of pressure support; however, only with
marginal oxygenation.

As the patient had an increasing white blood cell count, and
it was decided that he was going to need to have automatic
internal cardioverter-defibrillator placed to control his
ventricular arrhythmias, an Infectious Disease consultation
was obtained.  Their recommendations included continuing the
vancomycin, levofloxacin, ceftriaxone antibiotic regimen that
he was on while waiting for the blood cultures to be
finalized, as well as changing the site of his arterial line.

On postoperative day 12, the patient was weaned from his
ventilator and extubated without incident.  He was placed on
50% cool aerosol maintaining saturations of 97% to 100%
without any respiratory distress.

On postoperative day 13, the patient was seen by the Renal
Service for his rise in creatinine.  They felt that this
could most likely be explained by an acute event on [**9-4**]
when his creatinine bumped from 0.7 to 1.2 in the setting of
worsening ventricular tachycardia.  Initiation of Vasopressin
and the placement of the intra-aortic balloon pump.  It was
felt that he subsequently developed acute tubular necrosis at
that time.  Further diuresis was therefore avoided.

On [**9-14**], after having remained afebrile with a
decreasing white blood cell count the patient underwent the
placement of a [**Company 1543**] Model #7271, dual chamber,
implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well and was transferred back to the
Intensive Care Unit in stable condition.

By postoperative day 17, the patient continued to remain
afebrile and without any ventricular ectopy, with good
saturations and stable hemodynamics.  The decision was then
made to transfer the patient to the floor.

Once of the floor, the patient had an uncomplicated remainder
of his hospital course.  He had a chest x-ray on [**9-15**]
that demonstrated a lack of a pneumothorax.  His amiodarone
was discontinued.  His procainamide was changed to
Procanbid 1000 mg p.o. b.i.d.   Laboratories revealed a white
count of 8.8 and normal electrolytes.  He was satting 92% to
94% on room air.  His creatinine had dropped to 1.9.  The
patient was evaluated by the Physical Therapy Service who
felt that he would benefit from home physical therapy.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:  The patient was subsequently
discharged on [**9-17**] in stable condition with the plan
for physical therapy at home.

1.  Isordil 20 mg p.o. t.i.d.
2.  Protonix 40 mg p.o. q.d.
3.  Procanbid 1000 mg p.o. b.i.d.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION ON DISCHARGE:  The patient was afebrile
with stable vital signs.  He was alert and oriented.  His

systolic ejection murmur at the base.  His belly was soft,
nontender, and nondistended.  His extremities were warm and
well perfused.  His incisions were clean, dry and intact.

DISCHARGE STATUS:   The patient was discharged to home in

infiltrate, and the patient was continued on broad empiric
antibiotics for presumed community-acquired pneumonia.  The
patient continued with a 4-liter oxygen requirement on
transfer to the medicine floor.

afebrile on broad empiric antibiotics with no growth on
sputum, urine, as well as blood cultures.  The patient
continued with a large oxygen requirement with continued
right lower lobe infiltrate.

pulmonary examination and chest x-ray evidence of heart
failure at the time of admission.  The patient was diuresed
over the course of the hospital with significant improvement
in his symptoms and decreased oxygen needs.  The patient's
Lasix was titrated back down to his usual daily dose of 40 mg
p.o. q.d.

rehabilitation in stable condition.
